title: SHOULD WE BAPTIZE BABIES… OR ARE WE GIVING THEM A PROMISE THEY HAVEN’T YET BELIEVED?
paragraphs: SHOULD WE BAPTIZE BABIES… OR ARE WE GIVING THEM A PROMISE THEY HAVEN’T YET BELIEVED?

One baby. One baptism. Two sincere Christian convictions. And one question that forces us to examine what Scripture actually says about faith, grace, salvation, and the children we desperately want to see in heaven.
There is something about watching a baby being carried toward the waters of baptism that can make even the strongest heart tremble.
Tiny hands. Innocent eyes. A child who cannot yet pronounce the name of Jesus, much less explain the meaning of the cross.
A mother holds that child close.
A father stands beside her.
And somewhere in their hearts is a prayer they may never say aloud.
“Lord, whatever happens to me, please let my child know You.”
Then the water touches the baby's forehead.
For some Christians, it is a beautiful testimony to God's covenant promises, a sacred sign that His grace reaches toward us long before we understand it.
For others, something feels deeply unresolved.
How can someone be baptized before personally repenting? Before believing? Before confessing Jesus Christ as Lord?
And suddenly, a ceremony that should direct our hearts toward Christ becomes one of Christianity's most enduring disagreements.
But there is something more painful than Christians disagreeing about baptism.
It is the possibility that we become so determined to defend our tradition that we stop listening carefully to the Word of God.
Because the real question is not whether we love our children enough to baptize them.
The real question is whether we love Jesus enough to let Scripture challenge what we have always assumed.
And what we discover may be more uncomfortable, more beautiful, and more spiritually demanding than either side expects.
Before we go further, remember something.
The child in that mother's arms is not a theological argument.
That child is a human soul.
And the Savior at the center of this conversation is the same Jesus who welcomed little children when His own disciples tried to keep them away.
“Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.” — Mark 10:14, KJV
Jesus did not treat children as spiritual inconveniences.
He received them.
He blessed them.
He held them up as examples of the humble dependence that characterizes His kingdom.
But here is where we must be careful.
Mark 10 tells us that Jesus welcomed and blessed children. It does not explicitly say that He baptized them.
That distinction matters.
Because loving Scripture means refusing to make a passage say more than it actually says, even when the additional claim would support something we deeply believe.
And that brings us to a prison cell in Philippi.
A terrified man.
An earthquake.
An open door.
And one of the most important questions a human being can ever ask.
“Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” — Acts 16:30, KJV
Picture the scene.
It is midnight.
Paul and Silas have been beaten, imprisoned, and fastened in stocks. Their bodies are wounded, but their worship has not been silenced.
They are praying.
They are singing.
And then the earth begins to shake.
The prison doors open.
The chains come loose.
The jailer awakens to what appears to be a catastrophe. Believing the prisoners have escaped, he draws his sword to take his own life.
But Paul cries out.
“Do thyself no harm: for we are all here.” — Acts 16:28, KJV
Imagine hearing those words when you are one breath away from death.
The man who was supposed to guard the prisoners suddenly finds himself trembling before them.
And out of that fear comes a question far greater than his immediate circumstances.
“What must I do to be saved?”
Paul and Silas answer:
“Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and thou shalt be saved, and thy house.” — Acts 16:31, KJV
The Greek begins with a command:
Πίστευσον ἐπὶ τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν
Pisteuson epi ton kyrion Iēsoun Christon.
“Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.”
The verb pisteuson is a command addressed to the jailer. It calls him to place his trust in Christ.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not tell the jailer to trust in his ancestry.
He does not tell him to rely upon his religious upbringing.
He does not tell him that a ceremony, apart from Christ, can reconcile him to God.
He points him to Jesus.
But Paul also speaks of the jailer's household.
And this is where the discussion becomes fascinating.
Acts 16:32 says that Paul and Silas spoke the word of the Lord to the jailer and to all who were in his house.
Acts 16:33 says the jailer was baptized, along with all his household, without delay.
And Acts 16:34 describes the household rejoicing in connection with faith in God.

The Greek wording of verse 34 is important. The phrase pepisteukōs tō theō describes the jailer as having believed in God, while panoikei conveys a household-wide setting. Translators and interpreters differ over precisely how the rejoicing and believing should be understood in relation to every member of the household.
Now consider the two major interpretations.

Christians who practice infant baptism point out that entire households were baptized. They argue that the household language fits the biblical pattern of God's covenant dealings with families, even though the passage does not explicitly identify the ages of everyone present.

Christians who practice believer's baptism point to the proclamation of the Word, the command to believe, and the household's response. They understand the account as describing baptism following personal faith.
Both groups are observing something genuinely present in the text.
But neither should claim that Acts 16 explicitly tells us there was an infant in the jailer's household.
It does not.
Nor does the passage explicitly tell us there were no infants.
That silence must be respected.
And perhaps that is our first uncomfortable lesson.
Sometimes faithfulness requires us to say, “The Bible does not tell us everything we wish it did.”
That is not weakness.
That is reverence.
But the discussion does not end in Philippi.
It takes us much further back.
To Abraham.
To circumcision.
To a covenant promise.
And to the question of whether baptism is the New Testament counterpart to an ancient sign given even to children who could not yet understand it.
In Genesis 17, God commands Abraham to circumcise the males of his household, including infant boys eight days old.
These children did not first make a mature profession of faith.
The covenant sign was administered because they belonged to the covenant household.
For Christians in traditions that baptize infants, this becomes a significant part of the biblical argument.
They see continuity between God's covenant dealings with believers and their children under the old covenant and His dealings with the visible church under the new.
Then they turn to Colossians 2:11–12.
Paul writes:
Listen to the Greek expression:
περιτομῇ ἀχειροποιήτῳ
Peritomē acheiropoiētō.
“A circumcision made without hands.”
Paul is describing something far deeper than a physical operation.
A spiritual work accomplished through Christ.
The old covenant sign involved the flesh.
The inward reality Paul emphasizes involves the transforming work of God.
He then connects this spiritual circumcision with being buried and raised with Christ in baptism.
For infant-baptizing Christians, the connection is significant.

If children received the covenant sign under Abraham, and baptism now signifies incorporation into Christ and His covenant people, why should the children of believers be excluded from receiving the sign unless Scripture clearly excludes them?
That is a serious theological question.
It deserves a serious answer.
But Christians who practice believer's baptism respond with an equally important observation.
Colossians 2:12 explicitly mentions faith.
The Greek says:
διὰ τῆς πίστεως τῆς ἐνεργείας τοῦ θεοῦ
Dia tēs pisteōs tēs energeias tou theou.
“Through faith in the working of God.”
Paul is not merely describing the application of water.
He is describing union with Christ in His death and resurrection, received through faith in God's powerful work.

Believer's-baptism advocates therefore argue that the passage connects baptism with the believer's personal participation in Christ through faith, rather than establishing an instruction to baptize infants.

They also point out that circumcision and baptism are not identical in every respect. Circumcision was given specifically to males under the Abrahamic covenant, whereas Christian baptism is administered to males and females.
And while Colossians connects circumcision and baptism in its discussion of Christ, it does not explicitly command that baptism be administered to infants.
That matters too.
Here is the tension.
One side emphasizes the continuity of God's covenant promises.
The other emphasizes the new covenant's connection between faith and the baptismal sign.
Both appeal to Scripture.
Both seek to honor Christ.
And the disagreement cannot be settled merely by repeating one verse louder than the other.
It requires understanding the larger biblical story.
But there is another passage that deserves our attention.
On the day of Pentecost, Peter preaches Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
The people are pierced in their hearts.
They ask what they should do.
Peter answers:
“Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, and ye shall receive the gift of the Holy Ghost.” — Acts 2:38, KJV
Then he adds:
“For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call.” — Acts 2:39, KJV
Did you notice that?
“To your children.”
The Greek expression is:
τοῖς τέκνοις ὑμῶν
Tois teknois hymōn.
“To your children.”
For those who baptize infants, this language echoes the family-inclusive promises of God's covenant dealings.
They see a beautiful continuity: God's saving promises are proclaimed not only to individuals but also across generations.
But those who practice believer's baptism emphasize the rest of Peter's statement.
“Even as many as the Lord our God shall call.”

They argue that the promise reaches children and distant nations alike, but its saving fulfillment belongs to those whom God calls to Himself. They also point to Acts 2:41, where those who received Peter's message were baptized.
The text affirms that God's promise extends to the next generation.
It does not explicitly state whether infants should receive baptism before personally professing faith.
And again, faithful Christians must wrestle with the distinction between what Scripture explicitly teaches and what they infer from its wider covenant pattern.
Now perhaps someone reading this is thinking:
“I was baptized as a baby. Are you saying my baptism meant nothing?”
Someone else is thinking:
“My parents never baptized me. Did they fail me?”
And another person, perhaps a young mother, is quietly wondering:
“What if my child dies before being baptized?”
Please hear this carefully.
Your child's eternal destiny is not something you can control by performing a ceremony.
And the absence of a baptismal ceremony does not give any human being the authority to declare that a child is condemned.
Christians have developed different theological explanations concerning baptism, original sin, covenant membership, and the salvation of children who die young.
Those differences are real.
But Scripture never gives parents permission to replace trust in God's mercy with confidence in their own ability to perform every religious duty perfectly.
The Judge of all the earth will do what is right (Genesis 18:25).
Jesus is not less merciful than the parents who plead for their children.
And no parent should be pressured into thinking that purchasing spiritual security through a ritual is what saves a soul.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
This does not make baptism unimportant.
It makes Christ indispensable.
There is a difference.
Baptism is not a meaningless religious accessory.
Jesus commanded His disciples to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28:19).
In Romans 6:3–4, Paul describes baptism in connection with participation in Christ's death and resurrection, and the new life that follows.

In 1 Peter 3:21, Peter says that baptism saves, then immediately clarifies that he is not speaking about the removal of physical dirt but about an appeal or pledge toward God concerning a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The precise nuance of the Greek term eperōtēma is debated.
Christians understand the relationship between baptism, faith, and saving grace differently.
Some regard baptism as a means through which God ordinarily grants grace.
Others regard it as a commanded sign and public testimony of the grace received through faith.
But across these differences, a crucial Christian conviction remains:
The saving power is not found in water considered apart from Jesus Christ.
It is Christ who died for sinners.
Christ who rose from the grave.
Christ who reconciles us to the Father.
Christ who pours out the Holy Spirit.
Christ who calls us to repentance and faith.
And Christ who commands His church to make disciples.
This is why we must never confuse receiving a Christian ceremony with living as a disciple of Jesus.
A person may have been baptized in infancy and later abandon the faith entirely.
Another may have been baptized after professing faith and still live in open rebellion against God.
Neither person's outward history gives us permission to ignore the present condition of the heart.
That is the question that reaches beyond the theological debate and enters the room where you are sitting right now.
You may have been baptized before you could speak.
You may have been baptized after you walked down an aisle and publicly confessed Christ.
You may never have been baptized at all.
But let me ask you something more personal.
Do you know the Jesus whose name was spoken over the water?
Not merely His story.
Not merely the religious tradition of your family.
Not merely the church where your baptismal record is kept.
Do you know Him?
Have you come to recognize your sin?
Have you turned toward Him in repentance?
Are you trusting in His death and resurrection rather than your own goodness?
Because the danger is not simply that Christians may disagree about when baptism should happen.
The danger is that someone may spend an entire lifetime arguing about baptism while never surrendering to the Savior baptism proclaims.
Imagine standing before God and saying:
“But Lord, I was baptized.”
And discovering that you had spent your life trusting the memory of a ceremony instead of trusting Christ Himself.
Jesus warned that not everyone who calls Him “Lord” truly belongs to Him (Matthew 7:21–23).
That warning should humble every Christian, regardless of denomination.
But do not misunderstand it.
Jesus is not inviting us into despair.
He is inviting us out of false confidence and into genuine faith.
The same Christ who exposes empty religion welcomes repentant sinners.
The same Christ who confronts hypocrisy offers forgiveness.
The same Christ who calls us to follow Him gives grace to those who cannot save themselves.
That is the scandal of the Gospel.
The holy Son of God came for unholy people.
The sinless Savior bore the judgment sinners deserved.
The rejected Messiah became the hope of the rejected.
And the cross, which looked like the ultimate public humiliation, became the place where God's justice and mercy were displayed together.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Grace.
The Greek word is χάρις — charis.
God's favor, freely given, not earned by human merit.
It is not a reward for perfect parents.
Not a prize for belonging to the right family.
Not something purchased by a religious ceremony.
And not a license to ignore the commands of Jesus.
Saving grace brings us to Christ, and the grace that saves also begins transforming the life that receives it.
This is where our theme becomes more than a phrase.
He rewrites the story of the ashamed sinner who thought forgiveness was impossible.
He rewrites the story of the religious person who finally discovers that outward obedience cannot replace inward surrender.
He rewrites the story of the parent who fears that one imperfect decision has placed a beloved child beyond God's mercy.
And He can rewrite the story of the Christian who has spent years fighting other believers over baptism while neglecting the command to love one another.
Because being correct about a doctrine does not give us permission to become cruel.
And being loving does not give us permission to become careless with biblical truth.
We need both.
Truth without cruelty.
Love without compromise.
Conviction without arrogance.
Humility without abandoning Scripture.
So where does this leave the question?
Should Christians baptize infants, or only those who personally profess faith?
The answer depends on how one understands the relationship between the biblical covenants, the meaning of baptism, the nature of the visible church, and the role of personal faith.

Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Presbyterian, and other paedobaptist traditions have differing but substantial theological reasons for baptizing infants. They should not all be treated as though their explanations were identical. Some emphasize baptismal regeneration, while others emphasize covenant membership and God's promises without teaching that every baptized infant is thereby guaranteed salvation.
Baptist, many Pentecostal, and other credobaptist traditions understand the New Testament pattern as calling for baptism following a personal profession of faith.

The strongest straightforward argument for believer's baptism is the repeated New Testament pattern of the Gospel being preached, people responding in faith and repentance, and baptism following that response.

The strongest covenantal argument for infant baptism is the continuity of God's covenant dealings with believers and their children, together with household baptism accounts and the relationship between circumcision and baptism.
Neither Acts 16:30–34 nor Colossians 2:11–12 explicitly records an infant being baptized.
Neither passage, by itself, resolves every question raised by the wider covenant debate.

My conclusion from the explicit New Testament examples is that baptism following personal repentance and faith is the clearest directly demonstrated pattern. I find this the more persuasive practice because it closely follows the apostolic accounts of people hearing the Gospel, believing, and being baptized.

But I also recognize that thoughtful Christians who baptize infants are not necessarily dismissing faith or disregarding Scripture. They are drawing theological conclusions from a different understanding of covenant continuity.
That distinction should keep us from misrepresenting one another.

If you are a parent who believes infant baptism is biblically warranted, take seriously your responsibility to raise your child in the knowledge of Christ. Do not treat the baptism as a substitute for teaching, prayer, repentance, and lifelong discipleship.

If you are a parent who believes baptism should follow personal faith, dedicate yourself just as seriously to teaching your child the Scriptures, praying for their salvation, and preparing them to respond to the Gospel.
And if you are uncertain, study the relevant passages with your church leaders, examine the biblical arguments carefully, and seek to obey Christ with a clear conscience.
But whatever your position, do not forget the child.
That little boy will grow up.
That little girl will begin asking questions.
One day, the faith of the parents will be tested in the heart of the child.
There may be nights of rebellion.
Seasons of doubt.
Friends who mock Christianity.
Temptations that promise freedom while quietly building chains.
There may come a day when the child who once slept peacefully in a parent's arms says:
“I don't know if I believe in God anymore.”
And in that moment, the deepest concern of a Christian parent will not be winning an argument about the baptismal record.
It will be seeing that son or daughter come to know and love Jesus Christ.
So teach them the Gospel.
Let them see you repent when you are wrong.
Let them hear you pray when life is difficult.
Show them that Christianity is not merely a collection of rules but a life of trusting, obeying, and worshiping the living Savior.
Do not make the home a place where Jesus is mentioned constantly but His character is rarely reflected.
And never assume that because your child has participated in a Christian ritual, your responsibility to disciple them is finished.
The water may touch the body in a moment.
But discipleship reaches into a lifetime.
And this is where the argument about baptism should become a prayer for the next generation.
Lord, let our children know You.
Not simply know about You.
Not simply inherit our vocabulary.
Not simply repeat our denominational convictions.
Let them encounter the truth of Your Word, understand the Gospel, repent of sin, and trust in Jesus Christ.
Let their faith be genuine.
Let their obedience flow from love.
And when they wander, pursue them with Your truth and mercy.
If this article has exposed something in your own heart, don't hide behind a theological label.
Perhaps you have trusted your religious history more than Christ.
Perhaps you have judged Christians whose convictions differ from yours.
Perhaps you have neglected to teach your children the Gospel because you assumed their religious upbringing was enough.
Or perhaps you are a parent carrying a quiet fear for a child who has walked away from God.
You are welcome to share that burden here.

And if your heart is struggling with this question, tell us respectfully: Do you believe baptism should follow personal faith, or do you believe the covenant promises support infant baptism? What passage has most shaped your conviction?
Let the comments become a place for serious Scripture study, honest questions, testimonies, and prayer—not a battlefield where believers wound one another.
Someone reading your words may discover a passage they have never considered.
Someone may find the courage to open a Bible again.
Someone may finally realize that difficult theological questions do not have to drive them away from Christ.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win a debate.
But to invite them into the Word of God.
There is so much more to learn, and no believer should have to walk the journey of discipleship without encouragement.
These resources are offered to help believers study Scripture, deepen their prayer lives, strengthen their families, and grow in their understanding of Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading.
Consider helping us keep this work going.

Gospel Warrior is committed to proclaiming Christ, sharing Scripture, and making Christian resources accessible. Every article shared, every person encouraged, and every resource made available is part of that mission.
For those who choose to give regularly, that support can be an expression of Christian generosity and stewardship—an offering toward Gospel ministry, freely given according to conviction and ability.
Scripture says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Notice those words.
“Not grudgingly, or of necessity.”
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as a payment for God's favor, a requirement for salvation, or proof that someone truly loves Jesus.
It can help sustain the work and provide a foundation for future growth.
Not because God needs our money.
Not because grace has a price.
But because the work of creating, distributing, and expanding ministry resources involves real human effort and practical needs.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
The Gospel is not reserved for paying members.
The invitation to come to Christ is free.
And the glory belongs to God alone.
Before you leave, return with me to that prison in Philippi.
The jailer is trembling.
The doors are open.
The prisoners have not escaped.
And the question is still hanging in the darkness.
“What must I do to be saved?”
Imagine if Paul had responded by giving him a long explanation of why his family was more religious than another family.
Imagine if he had told him that belonging to the correct social group would make him acceptable to God.
Imagine if he had made the jailer's hope depend upon winning every theological debate.
But that is not what happened.
The answer began with Jesus.
“Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ.”
That same Jesus is still the center of our hope.
The One who welcomed children.
The One who called sinners to repentance.
The One who submitted to baptism and fulfilled all righteousness.
The One who carried our sins to Calvary.
The One who rose victorious from the grave.
The One who commands His people to make disciples and baptize them.
The One who will never be replaced by the ceremony that bears His name.
And perhaps the greatest question is not simply whether your baptism happened when you were eight days old, eight years old, or eighty years old.
Perhaps the question you must face today is this:
Have you entrusted your life to the Savior whom baptism points us toward?
Because your parents cannot repent in your place.
Your pastor cannot believe in your place.
Your religious heritage cannot love Jesus in your place.
And your baptismal certificate cannot substitute for a living relationship with the risen Christ.
Yet the Gospel offers extraordinary hope.
No matter how confused your religious past may be, you can turn to Jesus today.
No matter how many years you have lived without taking Him seriously, His call to repent and believe remains worthy of your response.
No matter how far your family has wandered, you can begin praying, teaching, loving, and pointing them toward Christ again.
And no matter which side of the baptism debate you stand on, you can kneel before the same crucified and risen Lord and ask Him to make your faith genuine.
The argument may continue.
The study must continue.
But let the church never forget why baptism matters in the first place.
It points us toward Jesus Christ and the salvation found in Him.
Because the greatest tragedy is not that someone might misunderstand the water, but that someone might spend a lifetime near the things of God and never truly turn to the Savior.
